response: Causal chain: (1) instruction present -> (2) after implementing, the agent enumerates boundary and degenerate input classes from the given list -> (3) it executes a check per class -> (4) failures on edge classes get fixed pre-completion -> (5) held-out pass rate rises because graders discriminate mainly on those classes. This mechanism REDIRECTS existing verification effort rather than adding a new stage, so its overhead cost is the lowest of the family and the counterfactual is crisp. The decisive assumption is the grader-discrimination profile: if baseline failures are whole-requirement omissions (never implemented a stated flag) rather than mishandled edges of implemented behavior, redirecting test effort cannot recover them. Supporting evidence: positive paired delta plus transcripts showing per-class executed checks; a failure-mode audit of baseline arms showing edge-class failures dominate. Disconfirming: baseline failure audit showing omitted-requirement dominance, or candidate transcripts with checklist-like shallow one-input-per-class checks and unchanged pass rate (compliance without intent).
